title: A strong acid and a weak acid at the same concentration

stimulus.title: Two acid solutions
stimulus.text: Flask 1 contains 50.0 mL of 0.050 M HNO₃. Flask 2 contains 50.0 mL of 0.050 M HNO₂ (Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴). Both are at 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the pH of the solution in each flask.

rubric.point: Flask 2: weak acid equilibrium, pH 2.37 (quadratic) or 2.35 (small x)

parts.sample: Flask 1: HNO₃ is strong, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.050 M and pH = 1.30. Flask 2: Ka = x²/(0.050 − x) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴. The small-x estimate, 4.5 × 10⁻³ M, is 9% of 0.050, so solve the quadratic: x = 4.3 × 10⁻³ M and pH = 2.37.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student says Flask 2 will need less NaOH to reach the equivalence point, because it has fewer H₃O⁺ ions. Do you agree or disagree? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Disagree: both contain 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol of acid; OH⁻ reacts with HNO₂ molecules as well as with H₃O⁺, so both need the same volume of NaOH
accept: disagree; same moles of acid, OH⁻ reacts with un-ionized HNO₂

parts.sample: Disagree. Each flask holds 0.0500 L × 0.050 M = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol of acid. OH⁻ takes protons directly from HNO₂ molecules (HNO₂ + OH⁻ → NO₂⁻ + H₂O goes to completion), not only from H₃O⁺, so both flasks need 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol of OH⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Each flask is diluted tenfold with water. Explain why the pH of Flask 2 rises by less than the pH of Flask 1.

rubric.point: Dilution makes Q < Ka for HNO₂, so a larger fraction ionizes, partly offsetting the dilution; the strong acid is already fully ionized, so its [H₃O⁺] falls tenfold
accept: percent ionization of the weak acid increases on dilution

parts.sample: HNO₃ is already fully ionized, so diluting tenfold lowers [H₃O⁺] tenfold and the pH rises by exactly 1.00. For HNO₂, diluting lowers all concentrations, making Q = [H₃O⁺][NO₂⁻]/[HNO₂] less than Ka, so more HNO₂ ionizes. That extra ionization partly replaces the lost H₃O⁺, so the pH rises by less than 1.
